howItWorks.intro: This calculator isolates the portion of your 401(k) actually exposed to a stock market decline — your balance multiplied by your stock allocation — then applies the drop percentage to that stock-exposed amount alone, not your whole account. From there it looks up how long declines of similar size have historically taken the S&P 500 to fully recover, and compounds today's paper loss forward at your expected return to show what an unrecovered loss could mean by your retirement date if it were never made up.
rules: Today's Loss = 401k Balance x Stock Allocation % x Market Drop %
Future Impact = Lost Amount x (1 + Avg Return)^Years (compounding the loss forward)
Recovery times based on historical S&P 500 drawdown analysis
Days of Contributions = Today's Loss / (Monthly Contribution / 22 workdays)
howItWorks.outro: These figures describe a snapshot in time, not a prediction and not a signal to act. Recovery timelines are drawn from past S&P 500 drawdowns, and markets do not repeat on schedule — a future decline could recover faster or slower than any historical average. This tool is meant to translate a scary headline into a concrete number for your own account, not to replace a conversation with a licensed financial advisor who knows your full retirement picture, timeline, and risk tolerance.

faq.question: Should I sell my 401(k) after a big market drop?
faq.answer: For most people still years from retirement, no. A drop only becomes a real, locked-in loss when you sell — until then it's a paper loss that recovers along with the market. Selling converts a temporary decline into a permanent one and forces you to guess correctly twice: once about when to get out, and again about when to get back in. The S&P 500 has recovered from every prior decline, including 2008 and 2020, but only for investors who stayed invested through the recovery.

faq.question: How long do market drops actually take to recover?
faq.answer: It scales with the size of the drop. Small pullbacks (5-10%) tend to resolve in weeks to a few months. The 2020 COVID crash — a roughly 34% peak-to-trough plunge in the S&P 500 — recovered in about five months, unusually fast because of aggressive stimulus. The 2022 bear market, an approximately 19% decline, took about two years to fully recover. The 2008 financial crisis was the outlier: a 37% drop that took over four years to reclaim its previous high. These are historical patterns, not promises about the next decline.

faq.question: Is a 401(k) balance drop a real loss if I don't sell?
faq.answer: No — as long as you hold your positions, a balance decline is an unrealized (paper) loss. It only becomes a realized loss if you sell your shares while they're worth less than you paid, or effectively lock it in by moving to cash near the bottom. If you keep contributing and stay invested, the shares you already own simply need the market to recover for the paper loss to close, and the shares you buy along the way are purchased at the lower, post-drop price.

faq.question: Should I keep contributing to my 401(k) during a downturn?
faq.answer: For anyone with more than a few years until they need the money, continuing — or even increasing — contributions during a drop is generally the higher-conviction move, not a riskier one. Every paycheck buys more shares per dollar while prices are down, a form of dollar-cost averaging that lowers your average cost basis and can accelerate how quickly your balance recovers once the market turns. Pausing contributions to wait it out means missing the cheapest purchase prices of the whole cycle.

faq.question: Why does this calculator ask about years to retirement?
faq.answer: Because the same dollar loss carries very different risk depending on your time horizon. Someone decades from retirement has time for both the market and their ongoing contributions to erase a drawdown. Someone within a few years of retiring — or already withdrawing — faces sequence-of-returns risk: a downturn that coincides with withdrawals forces you to sell more shares to generate the same income, permanently shrinking the portfolio even after the market eventually recovers. That's why near-retirees typically hold more in bonds and cash than someone in their 30s, cushioning exactly this scenario.

faq.question: Is this calculator giving me financial advice?
faq.answer: No. It applies straightforward arithmetic to the numbers you enter and pairs that with general, publicly documented historical patterns in U.S. stock market recoveries — it doesn't know your full financial picture, other accounts, debts, tax situation, or how close you actually are to needing this money. Treat the output as a starting point for your own thinking, and run any decision about selling, rebalancing, or changing your contribution rate past a licensed financial advisor who can look at your complete retirement plan.

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Measures
sections.body: A headline like "the S&P 500 fell 3% today" tells you almost nothing about your own account, because it treats your whole balance as if it were 100% invested in stocks. This calculator starts from your actual 401(k) or IRA balance, multiplies it by your stock allocation to isolate the dollars actually exposed to the drop, and only then applies the market's percentage decline. A $150,000 balance with 80% in stocks and a 3% market drop produces a $3,600 paper loss on $120,000 of stock exposure — not $4,500, which is what you'd get by incorrectly applying 3% to the whole account. The remaining 20% in bonds or cash typically moves far less, and often in the opposite direction, which is the entire point of holding it.

sections.title: Why Percentage Losses and Gains Aren't Symmetric
sections.body: Consider a $250,000 stock allocation hit by a 25% drop. The math is simple on the way down: $250,000 × 0.75 = $187,500, a $62,500 paper loss. Recovering that $62,500 is not a 25% problem anymore — it's a 33% problem, because $62,500 is 33.3% of the new, smaller $187,500 base, not of the original $250,000. This asymmetry is why deep drawdowns are so punishing, and why recovery time grows non-linearly as the drop size increases: a 10% correction typically needs about an 11% gain to break even, but a 50% crash needs a full 100% gain just to get back to where you started.

sections.title: Why This Hits Harder — Or Softer — Depending on Where You Are in Your Career
sections.body: The same 20% drop means something very different to a 30-year-old contributing $500 a month than it does to someone five years from retirement. For the 30-year-old, every dollar of decline buys more shares at a lower price through ongoing payroll contributions — dollar-cost averaging into a down market — and decades of compounding ahead absorb the setback. For someone close to retirement, a crash that lands just before or during the first years of withdrawals is far more dangerous: selling shares to cover living expenses while prices are down locks in losses that would otherwise have been temporary, and there's less runway left to rebuild. This is known as sequence-of-returns risk, and it's why advisors generally recommend shifting toward more bonds and cash — sometimes several years' worth of planned withdrawals — as retirement approaches, regardless of what an average-return assumption suggests you should expect in any single year.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator works in four passes, moving from a single day's paper loss to a full retirement-horizon projection.
steps: Multiply your 401(k)/IRA balance by your stock allocation percentage to isolate the dollars actually exposed to a stock market decline — the bond and cash portion is treated as unaffected by the day's drop.
Apply the market drop percentage to that stock-exposed amount to produce Today's Paper Loss — the actual dollar figure behind the headline percentage.

Match the size of the drop against historical S&P 500 drawdown-and-recovery patterns (5% dips, 10% corrections, 20% bear markets, 30%+ crashes like 2008 or 2020) to estimate a typical recovery window.

Compound today's loss forward at your expected average return across your years to retirement, so you can see what an unrecovered loss could mean at retirement age — alongside a separate projected balance that assumes the market recovers on its historical schedule and your contributions continue.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This tool runs the same arithmetic a financial planner might sketch on a napkin, but it can't see your full retirement picture — your other accounts, your actual risk tolerance, or how close you truly are to needing this money. Treat every number here as a planning estimate, not financial advice, and talk with a licensed financial advisor before changing your contributions, allocation, or holdings based on a single day's market move.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this calculator in the moment a market drop actually happens, not just during annual retirement planning.
scenarios: Right after a scary headline, to convert an abstract percentage ("the market fell 3% today") into the actual dollar number affecting your own balance.
Before deciding whether to sell, pause contributions, or move to cash during a downturn — to see the paper-loss math before making a permanent decision.
When you're within five to ten years of retirement and want to gauge how exposed your specific stock allocation is to a repeat of a 2008, 2020, or 2022-sized decline.
When deciding whether to keep dollar-cost averaging through a downturn, by comparing a projected balance with continued contributions against one where you stop.
When rebalancing after a big market move, to see what a further drop would now cost you given how far your allocation has drifted from target.

tips: Only your stock-allocated dollars move with a stock market headline — check your actual allocation percentage before assuming a 3% market drop means a 3% hit to your whole balance.

Recovery time grows faster than the drop size: a 10% correction typically needs about an 11% gain to break even, but a 40% decline needs a 67% gain — try a few drop percentages to see the curve for yourself.
If you're still contributing, a lower stock price isn't purely bad news — the same $500 contribution buys more shares in a downturn, which is dollar-cost averaging doing its job.
Sequence-of-returns risk bites hardest near retirement — if you're within about five years of needing the money, model a larger drop percentage here than you would for a 30-year horizon.
Run the calculator with your pre-drop balance and your post-drop balance side by side to see the recovery gain required, not just the loss — that number is usually the more sobering one.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your 401(k)/IRA Balance
howToSteps.description: Start with your current total balance across the retirement account you want to analyze — this is the base the calculator applies your stock allocation and the market drop to.

howToSteps.title: Set Your Stock Allocation
howToSteps.description: Enter the percentage of that balance currently invested in stocks versus bonds, cash, or stable-value funds. Check your plan's latest statement — target-date funds shift this percentage automatically as you age.

howToSteps.title: Enter the Market Drop Percentage
howToSteps.description: Type in the decline you want to model — either today's actual headline number or a hypothetical scenario like a 20% correction or a 2008-sized 37% crash — to see the dollar impact.

howToSteps.title: Enter Years to Retirement
howToSteps.description: This drives the future-impact projection, showing how today's loss would compound forward if it were never recovered, and how much time your account has left to bounce back.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Monthly Contribution
howToSteps.description: Include what you and your employer put in each month. Ongoing contributions during a downturn buy shares at the lower price, which feeds into your recovery projection.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Expected Average Return
howToSteps.description: Use a long-run assumption for your allocation — commonly 7-9% nominal for a stock-heavy portfolio — to compound both the loss and your projected balance forward realistically.

howToSteps.title: Review Your Results
howToSteps.description: Check Today's Paper Loss, the Stock Portion Affected, the Historical Recovery Time, and the two forward-looking projections side by side — together they show both what happened today and what it means, or doesn't, for your retirement date.
